# tweets/quote-of-post

Input: someone else's post (text, author, link) and the author's reaction to it. Output: a quote post whose comment transforms the original (reframes it, adds the missing datum, contradicts it with evidence), never a bare *this*, in the language of the post, and two lines under it: what it adds, and whether it passes the profile test.

The account is Yago Mendoza (@ymdatweets), an industrial engineer who builds with language models and writes about ML infrastructure, alignment, agent security and industrial systems. Tweets follow no canon: no style guide, and the writing rules of his site do not apply. Below is the account's strategy for this season. After this document the author may paste extra context for colour (his favourite expressions, sentences, moves, and what he does not want to sound like) and some of his own posted tweets: treat all of it as material, match that account (its topics, its humour, its way of stating things), and do not smooth it into a generic voice.

The site is public and you may browse it if you can: https://infraphysics.net. The wiki (every concept note, with search) is at https://infraphysics.net/wiki; a note's page is https://infraphysics.net/wiki/<slug>. Machine-readable copies: https://infraphysics.net/llms.txt lists every article and section, https://infraphysics.net/llms-full.txt carries the full text of every article, and https://infraphysics.net/wikinotes-index.json holds every wikinote's uid, name, address, aliases and description. Use them to check what already exists before linking, tagging or repeating it; never invent a note or a uid. When a tweet draws on one of his articles or notes, link the real page. Build it as the strategy's *The reply* section says: concede the frame, then take it further than its author did.

Remove these from anything you write here before showing it, in English or Spanish: dashes as pauses (em-dash, en dash, double hyphen: a parenthesis, a period or a comma instead, chosen per phrase); the *not X, Y* reframe (*it's not about speed, it's about trust*: say the thing); the mic-drop line after a wind-up (*That's it.*); section selling (*here's where it gets interesting*); metacommentary on your own posture (*let me be direct*, *to be honest*); performed casualness (*vibes*, *rent-free*, *let that sink in*); the tricolon for gravitas; throat-clearing (*it's worth noting*, *furthermore*, *in summary*, *ultimately*); the hedged ending; decorated numbers (*an impressive 23%*); double quotes around a term (italics); arrows between concepts. When one appears, rebuild the sentence around what it was trying to say; never swap one tic for another, and never remove specificity to add polish.

## `_studio/twitter/STRATEGY.md`

## Twitter: strategy

> What the account is doing this season and why. Written from a conversation with a model on 2026-09-11 (starting point: 123 followers), checked against the public code of X's feed. It changes when the phase changes. There is no style file next to it on purpose: tweets follow no canon.

### The one idea

The personality does not change as followers grow. What changes, progressively, is the source of distribution: from borrowing it (replying inside conversations that already have traffic) to generating it (posting ideas that get signal on their own). The mix of topics and the voice start now, at 123, so that whoever follows for a meme discovers over time that the account also builds agents, comes from industrial engineering, writes essays and has its own ideas about technology. No shitposting to a thousand and a sudden turn into the serious researcher.

One milestone is not arbitrary: the published feed code keeps a cold-start boost for authors up to 1,000 followers, aimed at posts with few impressions ([author_cold_start.rs](https://github.com/xai-org/x-algorithm/blob/main/home-mixer/scorers/author_cold_start.rs), [param.rs](https://github.com/xai-org/x-algorithm/blob/main/home-mixer/params/param.rs)). The first thousand play under different rules.

### Phases

1. **Now, 123 to 500: discovery.** Appear often in conversations that already have traffic. Roughly one own post a day when there is one (never to fill a slot), three to six good replies to people in AI, engineering and science who are getting attention: a meme, an observation, a datum, a small contradiction, an image. Replies that could have been posts. Quote posts when the comment transforms the original, never a bare *this*. If a reply with an image is especially good, repost it once so it also lives on the timeline. Few plain reposts of others: the profile must look like someone who produces, not a curator.
2. **500 to 1,000: recognise the patterns.** Same formula; start identifying which version of the account attracts strangers (memes about AI, technical opinions, small philosophical observations, agents, essays). Double down on formats, not on tweets: if *the fly* works, do not post five flies; learn that *a cultural image of the moment plus a very specific AI observation plus dry humour* works. Aim for half or more of what a visitor sees on the profile to be original.
3. **1,000 to 5,000: depend less on replies.** The explicit small-author boost ends around here, the first change with a concrete algorithmic reason. People start recognising the handle. Move to about 70% own posts and quotes, 30% strategic replies. Post small quotable ideas: a strong observation in one to three sentences, a capture of something being built, an agent experiment, a meme, occasionally an essay. Start getting others to reply to the account instead of always replying to others.
4. **5,000 to 20,000: a small personal medium.** Fewer opportunistic replies; still answer interesting people, because the conversation is wanted, not because they have 300K views. The advantage now is that an idea published directly has enough initial audience to get signal. Recurring formats without calling them series: experiments, diagrams, small things learned building agents, industrial oddities, observations on AI, strong fragments of InfraPhysics. Essays launch on their own thesis.
5. **20,000 and up: stop optimising visibly.** The phase where everything should look most natural: own posts, conversations, some nonsense, serious work, photos, things found. If every tweet looks designed for engagement the account loses what made it interesting. Distribution now also comes from being the node others reply to and quote.

In one line: up to 1K, enter conversations; 1K to 5K, turn attention into identity; 5K and up, make the conversations start around the account.

### Tomorrow, literally

One own post that deserves to exist, three to five really good replies in conversations of the niche, maybe one quote if something perfect appears. Not volume: five memorable interventions beat twenty-five filler replies.

The brutal rule before replying to a big post: *if someone sees only my reply and opens my profile, have I given them a reason to follow?* If not, the reply does not serve the goal.

### The reply

The role: the ideal third participant. Two positions are already on the table; the reply understands both, adds the one variable that was missing, and leaves two or three places where a fourth person can continue. Not the smartest comment: the one an interesting technician would leave almost without effort, and that would give a stranger who opens the profile a reason to follow.

Shape: concede the other's frame, then the concrete problem from own experience, then one image that compresses the reasoning, then the inversion (the memorable line), then the consequence, and stop before explaining. Roughly 70% extending the thesis, 30% friction: *yes, and if that holds, this follows*, never *this is wrong*. Take the premise further than its author did, to the uncomfortable place it was not mentioning.

Language: one precise term named correctly (*harness*) and ordinary words around it; no paper vocabulary (*sequential depth*, *causal non-identifiability*, *verification loops*). Competence shows in the single observation only someone who builds these things would make (the designer's categories and the optimiser's do not coincide), never in a list. Humour comes from register, not jokes: something technical described in domestic or administrative words (*four rules, some tools and a perimeter*, *putting zip ties on it*, *looking for gaps*), no elaborate metaphors, no punchlines. Mix, roughly: 60% plain engineering language, 25% physical everyday Spanish, 10% anglicisms the sector really uses, 5% oddity.

Kills, each one removing a whole family of replies: student questions, interview questions, lists of controls, anything that says *look, I know this*, going against the premise, trying to be funny, ideas transportable to any thread (the reply must depend on this post's frame).

### What to measure

Not followers alone. Watch for likes, replies, quotes and follows from people who did not already follow: that is the sign of leaving the initial graph. The feed mixes in-network and out-of-network content and ranks it by predicted actions ([x-algorithm](https://github.com/xai-org/x-algorithm)), so the target is pieces that get signal outside the starting audience. A format that produced that once goes into `posted/` with a note saying so, and the note is all the record it needs.
